fields.definition: The real-time balancing of a musical performance's audio for a live television broadcast, combining stage, vocal, and ambience sources into a program mix delivered to the transmission/air chain while meeting broadcast loudness targets.
fields.plain_english: It is mixing music live for a TV show while it airs. The engineer blends the band, singers, and crowd into one balanced sound that goes out right away.
fields.purpose_function: Gives viewers a polished, consistent music mix in real time and keeps program loudness within broadcast limits.
fields.practical_application: A broadcast mixer builds this on a console during live events such as awards shows or concerts, riding faders and effects as the show happens.
common_mistakes: Ignoring broadcast loudness targets so the mix is too loud or too quiet next to other programming
Burying dialogue or vocals under music and crowd sound
Not building a backup or safety mix in case a key source fails
scenario_contexts: Mixing a live awards-show music performance for network TV
Balancing a house band and audience mics during a late-night talk show
Sending a music mix from an OB truck to master control

sources: ATSC A/85 (Techniques for Establishing and Maintaining Audio Loudness for Digital Television)

fields.definition: The audio mix prepared specifically for an internet live stream, blending program sources into a stereo or immersive feed sent to the streaming encoder, typically metered to the platform's loudness target and kept separate from the PA or broadcast mix.
fields.plain_english: It is the sound mix made just for a live internet stream. It blends the sources into one feed for the stream, which is often different from what the room speakers or a TV feed get.
fields.purpose_function: Gives online viewers a clear, balanced sound and holds stream loudness steady, independent of the venue's live PA mix.
fields.practical_application: A streaming engineer sets this up on a console send or a separate mixer, feeding the encoder while checking level on headphones and meters.
common_mistakes: Sending the raw PA mix to the stream, which often sounds unbalanced to online listeners
Letting loudness drift so the stream is much louder or quieter than other content
Not checking mono compatibility for phone listeners
scenario_contexts: Streaming a church service or concert to an online platform
Mixing a webcast panel on a separate bus from the room PA
Feeding a dedicated stream mix to an encoder in an OB truck

fields.definition: A broadcast-automation operating mode in which a live operator manually starts each on-air element while the automation system loads, cues, and logs the playlist; a middle ground between fully automated playout and fully manual live operation.
fields.plain_english: It is a radio mode where the computer lines up the songs and clips, but a person presses start for each one. The machine does the prep work while the operator controls the timing live.
fields.purpose_function: Lets a live host keep hands-on control of pacing and talk-ups while the automation handles queuing, logging, and file playback.
fields.practical_application: A board operator uses this during live shows, hitting play or a segue button as the system stands ready with the next scheduled items.
common_mistakes: Assuming the system will auto-segue and missing a manual start, which causes dead air
Not watching the queue, so wrong or out-of-order elements play
Forgetting to reconcile the as-run log after manual changes
scenario_contexts: A morning-show host driving the board in assist mode during a music sweep
Manually firing news and weather inserts between automated songs
Taking manual control to extend a live interview past its scheduled slot

fields.definition: The central technical hub of a broadcast facility where program signals from studios, networks, and remote sources are routed, monitored, switched, and readied for transmission to the transmitter or distribution network; the final quality-control point of the air chain.
fields.plain_english: It is the control hub of a TV or radio station. Every program signal passes through here to be checked and switched before it goes out to the audience.
fields.purpose_function: Acts as the final gatekeeper of the air chain, making sure the correct program, at the right level and quality, reaches the transmitter or network.
fields.practical_application: A master control operator watches monitors and meters here, switches sources, inserts commercials and station IDs, and responds to alarms or signal faults.
common_mistakes: Confusing master control with a production control room; master control handles transmission, not show production
Missing a loudness or level problem before it reaches air
UNSAFE: Assuming transmitter or power gear is de-energized; work on such equipment requires lockout/tagout and station safety procedures
scenario_contexts: Switching from a network feed to local news at the top of the hour
Rolling a scheduled commercial break and station ID
Responding to a loss-of-signal alarm on the air chain

fields.definition: A vehicle outfitted as a self-contained mobile control room for recording or broadcasting events at remote locations, housing mixing consoles, routing, monitoring, communications, and often transmission or recording equipment; also called an outside-broadcast (OB) truck or remote production unit.
fields.plain_english: It is a truck built as a rolling control room. Crews drive it to concerts or games and mix, record, or broadcast the event from inside it.
fields.purpose_function: Brings a full production and control facility to venues that have no fixed studio, so remote events can be recorded or aired.
fields.practical_application: An audio engineer works from the truck's console, taking splits from stage mics and sending finished mixes back to the network or a recorder.
common_mistakes: UNSAFE: Powering the truck from site mains without proper grounding and bonding and a verified safe connection
Underestimating the cable runs and mic splits needed between stage and truck
Not coordinating comms and tie-lines with the venue and network early
scenario_contexts: Broadcasting a live sports game from a stadium compound
Recording a multitrack concert for later release
Providing a mobile mix for a remote awards ceremony

fields.definition: A small, acoustically treated studio space used to record or broadcast spoken news segments, voice-overs, and updates, typically equipped with a microphone, headphones, a small mixer or interface, and a talkback link to the control room.
fields.plain_english: It is a small, quiet room for reading the news on air. It has a mic and headphones and keeps outside noise out so the voice sounds clean.
fields.purpose_function: Gives news readers an isolated, quiet space so recorded or live voice reports sound clear and free of background noise.
fields.practical_application: A reporter or anchor uses the booth to voice bulletins and inserts, cueing off the control room and monitoring their own level in headphones.
common_mistakes: Working too close to the mic without a pop filter, causing plosives and distortion
Ignoring room noise such as HVAC that the treatment does not fully block
Setting the level too hot and clipping the interface
scenario_contexts: Voicing an hourly radio news update
Recording a news insert to drop into a later bulletin
Doing a live two-way with the main studio from the booth

fields.definition: A pre-recorded or remotely originated news segment, such as a reporter's package, actuality, or bulletin, played into a live program or newscast at a scheduled point in the running order.
fields.plain_english: It is a ready-made news clip dropped into a show. The clip, like a reporter's report, plays at a set spot in the running order.
fields.purpose_function: Lets stations add prepared or field-sourced news content into live programming without interrupting the studio flow.
fields.practical_application: An operator or presenter fires the insert on cue from the playout system or console, then returns to the live studio.
common_mistakes: Firing the insert at the wrong time or over live speech
Not checking the insert's level and loudness against the program
Forgetting to update the running order so the insert is skipped or doubled
scenario_contexts: Playing a reporter's package during the evening newscast
Dropping a recorded news bulletin between automated music tracks
Rolling an actuality clip during a live interview

fields.definition: A monitoring device or feed that receives and demodulates the station's actual transmitted (off-air) signal, letting operators confirm what is genuinely being broadcast rather than only the console or pre-transmission output; used for confidence and compliance checking.
fields.plain_english: It is a receiver that listens to what the station is really putting out on air. It lets staff check the true broadcast, not just the signal before it leaves the building.
fields.purpose_function: Confirms the transmitted signal is present and correct, catching faults that occur after the console but before or at the transmitter.
fields.practical_application: An operator checks the off-air monitor to verify audio is actually going out, comparing it against the studio feed for delay, dropout, or quality problems.
common_mistakes: Trusting only the console meter and missing a fault that appears after transmission
Confusing the delayed off-air return with the live studio feed while talking on air
Not accounting for the transmission delay when comparing feeds
scenario_contexts: Verifying the transmitter is passing audio during a live show
Catching a silent transmitter while the console still shows signal
Comparing off-air quality after a processing or antenna change

fields.definition: The broadcast studio currently originating live programming and feeding the air chain, equipped with the on-air console, microphones, playout, and monitoring from which presenters host and control the live output.
fields.plain_english: It is the studio that is live on air right now. The host sits here and controls the show that listeners or viewers are getting.
fields.purpose_function: Serves as the origination point for live programming, giving the presenter the console and tools to control what goes to air.
fields.practical_application: A presenter or board operator runs the show from here, opening mics, playing elements, and segueing while monitoring the output.
common_mistakes: Leaving a mic open when it should be closed, putting unwanted audio on air
Not confirming this studio is actually the one switched to air before speaking
UNSAFE: Ignoring high headphone or monitor levels that risk hearing damage over long shifts
scenario_contexts: Hosting a live morning radio show
Anchoring a live TV news segment
Switching air origination from one studio to another between programs
